Operators 1: Matrices and Dirac Notation

What you need to know

  • An operator turns one function into another. Quantum operators are linear, so they respect superposition: acting on a sum gives the sum of the results.

  • A matrix is the linear operator you already know: it turns and stretches arrows. The arrows it only stretches are its eigenvectors, Av=λvA\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv, and for a 2×22\times 22×2 matrix the eigenvalues come from a quadratic equation.

  • Sample a function on a grid and it becomes a vector; every operator becomes a matrix. Position is diagonal, derivatives link neighboring points, and solving H^ψ=Eψ\hat{H}\psi = E\psiH^ψ=Eψ becomes finding the eigenvalues of a matrix: by hand for three points, with five lines of numpy for four hundred.

  • Dirac notation writes the same objects once. A ket is a column, a bra is the conjugated row, a bra meeting a ket is an inner product, and a bra, an operator and a ket together give a matrix element. Every line translates into an integral and into numpy.

  • The entries of a matrix depend on the axes you write it in. In the axes of its own eigenvectors a matrix is diagonal, with the eigenvalues on the diagonal, and finding those axes is what diagonalizing a Hamiltonian means.

  • Two matrix properties matter next: some matrices equal their own mirror image (Hermitian), and the order of a product can matter (commutators). Both are the subject of Operators 2.

The rules of the game¶

This lecture and the next three complete the short list of rules, the postulates, from which all of quantum mechanics follows. Two of them we have already met.

PostulateLecture
1The state of a system is a wavefunction ψ\psiψ, and ∣ψ∣2\lvert\psi\rvert^2∣ψ∣2 is the probability densityThe Schrödinger Equation
2Every observable is represented by a linear Hermitian operator A^\hat{A}A^this lecture and Operators 2
3A measurement of AAA returns one of the eigenvalues ana_nan​ of A^\hat{A}A^ and leaves the system in its eigenfunction ϕn\phi_nϕn​Measurement
4The outcome ana_nan​ has probability ∣⟨ϕn∣ψ⟩∣2\lvert\langle \phi_n \vert \psi\rangle\rvert^2∣⟨ϕn​∣ψ⟩∣2, so the average is ⟨A⟩=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩\langle A\rangle = \langle \psi \vert \hat{A} \vert \psi \rangle⟨A⟩=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩Measurement
5The state evolves by iℏ ∂Ψ/∂t=H^Ψi\hbar\,\partial\Psi/\partial t = \hat{H}\Psiiℏ∂Ψ/∂t=H^ΨThe Schrödinger Equation, Time Dependence

Operators act on functions¶

  • In The Schrödinger Equation we built operators by a recipe: write the classical expression in xxx and ppp, then replace ppp by −iℏ d/dx-i\hbar\,d/dx−iℏd/dx. We also met eigenfunctions, the functions an operator returns unchanged up to a constant, and expectation values.

  • The recipe leaves two questions open: which operators are allowed to stand for something we can measure, and what happens when two operators do not commute? Operators 2 answers both. This lecture builds the language they need: functions become vectors, and operators become matrices.

  • An operator is any rule that turns a function into another function: multiply by xxx, differentiate, integrate, square. Quantum mechanics uses only one kind.

Linear operators¶

Linear operator
A^ (c1ψ1+c2ψ2)=c1 A^ψ1+c2 A^ψ2\hat{A}\,\big(c_1\psi_1 + c_2\psi_2\big) = c_1\,\hat{A}\psi_1 + c_2\,\hat{A}\psi_2A^(c1​ψ1​+c2​ψ2​)=c1​A^ψ1​+c2​A^ψ2​
(1)

for any functions ψ1\psi_1ψ1​, ψ2\psi_2ψ2​ and any complex numbers c1c_1c1​, c2c_2c2​.

  • Linearity is what superposition demands. If Ψ1\Psi_1Ψ1​ and Ψ2\Psi_2Ψ2​ both solve iℏ ∂Ψ/∂t=H^Ψi\hbar\,\partial\Psi/\partial t = \hat{H}\Psiiℏ∂Ψ/∂t=H^Ψ, their sum is again a solution only when H^\hat{H}H^ is linear. Interference, from the double slit to the sloshing particle in a box, shows that sums of states are states, so the operators must be linear.

  • Derivatives and multiplication by a function are linear: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Squaring, square roots and logarithms are not.

Example: two tests for linearity

Is the kinetic energy operator K^=−ℏ22md2dx2\hat{K} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}K^=−2mℏ2​dx2d2​ linear? Is squaring, S^f=f2\hat{S}f = f^2S^f=f2?

K^(c1f1+c2f2)=−ℏ22m(c1f1′′+c2f2′′)=c1K^f1+c2K^f2\hat{K}\big(c_1f_1 + c_2f_2\big) = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\big(c_1f_1'' + c_2f_2''\big) = c_1\hat{K}f_1 + c_2\hat{K}f_2K^(c1​f1​+c2​f2​)=−2mℏ2​(c1​f1′′​+c2​f2′′​)=c1​K^f1​+c2​K^f2​
(2)

so K^\hat{K}K^ is linear. For squaring,

S^(c1f1+c2f2)=c12f12+2c1c2f1f2+c22f22≠c1f12+c2f22\hat{S}\big(c_1f_1 + c_2f_2\big) = c_1^2f_1^2 + 2c_1c_2f_1f_2 + c_2^2f_2^2 \ne c_1f_1^2 + c_2f_2^2S^(c1​f1​+c2​f2​)=c12​f12​+2c1​c2​f1​f2​+c22​f22​=c1​f12​+c2​f22​
(3)

The squared constants and the cross term 2c1c2f1f22c_1c_2f_1f_22c1​c2​f1​f2​ both spoil it. A quick first test: a linear operator must turn 2f2f2f into 2A^f2\hat{A}f2A^f, and squaring turns it into 4f24f^24f2.

Matrices act on vectors¶

The linear operators you already know are matrices. Before turning functions into vectors, here is what a matrix does to an ordinary arrow in the plane. Vectors and Linear Algebra in Appendix A has more.

  • A matrix acts on a vector row by column: each entry of the result is one row of the matrix times the column, entry by entry, added up. For A=(2112)A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​),

A(10)=(2⋅1+1⋅01⋅1+2⋅0)=(21),A(11)=(33)=3(11)A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = 3\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}A(10​)=(2⋅1+1⋅01⋅1+2⋅0​)=(21​),A(11​)=(33​)=3(11​)
(4)

  • The first arrow is turned as well as stretched. The second keeps its direction and is only stretched, by a factor of 3.

Fig. The matrix AAA turns a generic arrow (left) but only stretches its eigenvectors (right): (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) by a factor 3 and (1,−1)(1, -1)(1,−1) by a factor 1.

Try it: drag anywhere on the plane to aim the unit arrow v\mathbf{v}v and watch AvA\mathbf{v}Av. Most directions come out turned. Hunt for the two directions that are only stretched; the widget marks each one you find. Sweep carries v\mathbf{v}v once around the circle, pausing on each eigenvector, while the tips of AvA\mathbf{v}Av trace an ellipse.

Eigenvectors and eigenvalues of a matrix
Av=λv,v≠0⟺det⁡(A−λI)=0A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, \quad \mathbf{v} \neq 0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \det(A - \lambda I) = 0Av=λv,v=0⟺det(A−λI)=0
(5)

  • This has the same shape as the eigenvalue equation A^ϕ=aϕ\hat{A}\phi = a\phiA^ϕ=aϕ of The Schrödinger Equation, with a matrix in place of the operator and a vector in place of the function.

  • Why the determinant? (A−λI)v=0(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = 0(A−λI)v=0 says that the matrix A−λIA - \lambda IA−λI squashes the nonzero arrow v\mathbf{v}v to zero. A matrix that squashes some arrow to zero flattens the plane, so the area factor it multiplies areas by, its determinant, is zero. For a 2×22\times 22×2 matrix the condition is a quadratic equation:

det⁡(a−λbcd−λ)=(a−λ)(d−λ)−bc=λ2−(a+d) λ+(ad−bc)=0\det\begin{pmatrix} a - \lambda & b \\ c & d - \lambda \end{pmatrix} = (a - \lambda)(d - \lambda) - bc = \lambda^2 - (a + d)\,\lambda + (ad - bc) = 0det(a−λc​bd−λ​)=(a−λ)(d−λ)−bc=λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−bc)=0
(6)

  • The roots of λ2−sλ+p=0\lambda^2 - s\lambda + p = 0λ2−sλ+p=0 add up to sss and multiply to ppp. So the eigenvalues of a 2×22\times 22×2 matrix add up to a+da + da+d, the sum of its diagonal entries, called the trace, and multiply to ad−bcad - bcad−bc, the determinant. These two numbers give a quick check on any eigenvalue calculation.

Example: eigenvalues of a 2×22\times 22×2 by hand

Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A=(2112)A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​).

det⁡(A−λI)=(2−λ)2−1=0⟹2−λ=±1⟹λ=3, 1\det(A - \lambda I) = (2 - \lambda)^2 - 1 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2 - \lambda = \pm 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = 3,\ 1det(A−λI)=(2−λ)2−1=0⟹2−λ=±1⟹λ=3, 1
(7)

For λ=3\lambda = 3λ=3, the first row of (A−3I)v=0(A - 3I)\mathbf{v} = 0(A−3I)v=0 reads −v1+v2=0-v_1 + v_2 = 0−v1​+v2​=0, so v∝(1,1)\mathbf{v} \propto (1, 1)v∝(1,1). For λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 it reads v1+v2=0v_1 + v_2 = 0v1​+v2​=0, so v∝(1,−1)\mathbf{v} \propto (1, -1)v∝(1,−1). Two quick checks: the eigenvalues add up to the trace, 3+1=2+23 + 1 = 2 + 23+1=2+2, and multiply to the determinant, 3×1=2⋅2−1⋅13 \times 1 = 2\cdot 2 - 1\cdot 13×1=2⋅2−1⋅1.

From operators to matrices¶

A computer cannot store a function, only a list of numbers. Turning functions into lists and operators into tables of numbers is how every quantum chemistry program works, and it makes the abstract properties of operators, Hermitian or commuting, concrete enough to check by eye. We build the dictionary in four steps. Operators as Matrices in Appendix A has more on each.

Step 1: a function becomes a vector¶

  • Pick NNN grid points x1,x2,…,xNx_1, x_2, \dots, x_Nx1​,x2​,…,xN​ spaced hhh apart and record the value of the function at each one, ψj=ψ(xj)\psi_j = \psi(x_j)ψj​=ψ(xj​). The function becomes a column of NNN numbers.

Source

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

xs = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)
f = lambda x: np.sin(np.pi * x) + 0.45 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
N, h = 7, 1 / 8
xj = h * np.arange(1, N + 1); fj = f(xj)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.7))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 3, width_ratios=[2.6, 0.5, 0.9], wspace=0.05)

ax.plot(xs, f(xs), color=TEAL, lw=2.6, label=r"$\psi(x)$")
ax.vlines(xj, 0, fj, color=GRAY, lw=1, ls=":")
ax.plot(xj, fj, "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=8, zorder=5)
for j, (xv, fv) in enumerate(zip(xj, fj), start=1):
    ax.text(xv, fv + 0.09, rf"$\psi_{j}$", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=CARDINAL)
ax.plot([0, 0], [0, 1.55], color="k", lw=2.6); ax.plot([1, 1], [0, 1.55], color="k", lw=2.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8)
ax.annotate("", xy=(xj[3], -0.14), xytext=(xj[2], -0.14), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="k", lw=1.2))
ax.text((xj[2] + xj[3]) / 2, -0.2, r"$h$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=13)
ax.set_xlim(-0.03, 1.03); ax.set_ylim(-0.42, 1.6)
ax.set_xticks(list(xj)); ax.set_xticklabels([rf"$x_{j}$" for j in range(1, N + 1)], fontsize=12)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False); ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(length=0)
ax.set_title(r"a function, sampled at $N$ points spaced $h$ apart", loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
axa.axis("off")
axa.annotate("", xy=(0.95, 0.5), xytext=(0.05, 0.5), xycoords="axes fraction",
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="simple,head_length=0.8,head_width=0.8,tail_width=0.3", color=PURPLE, alpha=0.8))
axv.axis("off"); axv.set_xlim(0, 1); axv.set_ylim(0, N + 1)
for j, fv in enumerate(fj, start=1):
    y = N + 0.5 - j
    axv.text(0.5, y, f"{fv:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,

    axv.text(0.02, y, rf"$\psi_{j}$", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=11, color=CARDINAL)
axv.plot([0.27, 0.22, 0.22, 0.27], [N + 0.35, N + 0.35, 0.15, 0.15], color="k", lw=1.4)
axv.plot([0.73, 0.78, 0.78, 0.73], [N + 0.35, N + 0.35, 0.15, 0.15], color="k", lw=1.4)
axv.set_title("a vector", fontsize=12.5)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.99, top=0.88, bottom=0.12)

Fig. A wavefunction in a box sampled at seven interior points. The walls, where ψ=0\psi = 0ψ=0, carry no unknowns. The seven samples, stacked in a column, are the vector that stands in for the function.

  • Integrals become sums. The inner product of two functions becomes the dot product of their vectors, times the spacing:

∫ϕ∗ ψ dx  ≈  ∑jϕj∗ ψj h,∫∣ψ∣2 dx=1  ⟶  ∑j∣ψj∣2 h=1\int \phi^*\,\psi\,dx \;\approx\; \sum_{j} \phi_j^*\,\psi_j\,h, \qquad \int \lvert\psi\rvert^2\,dx = 1 \;\longrightarrow\; \sum_j \lvert\psi_j\rvert^2\,h = 1∫ϕ∗ψdx≈j∑​ϕj∗​ψj​h,∫∣ψ∣2dx=1⟶j∑​∣ψj​∣2h=1
(8)

Step 2: multiplying by xxx is a diagonal matrix¶

  • x^\hat{x}x^ multiplies the value at each point by that point’s own position, (x^ψ)j=xj ψj(\hat{x}\psi)_j = x_j\,\psi_j(x^ψ)j​=xj​ψj​. As a matrix acting on the vector, every entry off the diagonal is zero:

x^ ψ  ⟶  (x10000x20000x30000x4)(ψ1ψ2ψ3ψ4)=(x1ψ1x2ψ2x3ψ3x4ψ4)\hat{x}\,\psi \;\longrightarrow\; \begin{pmatrix} x_1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & x_2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & x_3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & x_4 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \psi_1 \\ \psi_2 \\ \psi_3 \\ \psi_4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x_1\psi_1 \\ x_2\psi_2 \\ x_3\psi_3 \\ x_4\psi_4 \end{pmatrix}x^ψ⟶⎝⎛​x1​000​0x2​00​00x3​0​000x4​​⎠⎞​⎝⎛​ψ1​ψ2​ψ3​ψ4​​⎠⎞​=⎝⎛​x1​ψ1​x2​ψ2​x3​ψ3​x4​ψ4​​⎠⎞​
(9)

  • Any potential works the same way: V^\hat{V}V^ is the diagonal matrix of V(x1),…,V(xN)V(x_1), \dots, V(x_N)V(x1​),…,V(xN​). Multiplying by a function never mixes different points.

Step 3: derivatives compare neighbors¶

  • A derivative is a slope, and a slope needs two points. The centered difference uses the two neighbors of xjx_jxj​. For the second derivative, take the change between the slopes on either side, s+=(ψj+1−ψj)/hs_+ = (\psi_{j+1} - \psi_j)/hs+​=(ψj+1​−ψj​)/h and s−=(ψj−ψj−1)/hs_- = (\psi_j - \psi_{j-1})/hs−​=(ψj​−ψj−1​)/h, per unit length:

ψ′(xj)≈ψj+1−ψj−12h,ψ′′(xj)≈s+−s−h=ψj+1−2ψj+ψj−1h2\psi'(x_j) \approx \frac{\psi_{j+1} - \psi_{j-1}}{2h}, \qquad \psi''(x_j) \approx \frac{s_+ - s_-}{h} = \frac{\psi_{j+1} - 2\psi_j + \psi_{j-1}}{h^2}ψ′(xj​)≈2hψj+1​−ψj−1​​,ψ′′(xj​)≈hs+​−s−​​=h2ψj+1​−2ψj​+ψj−1​​
(10)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
f = lambda x: 0.75 + 0.42 * np.sin(1.7 * x - 0.6) + 0.06 * x
df = lambda x: 0.42 * 1.7 * np.cos(1.7 * x - 0.6) + 0.06
xs = np.linspace(-0.2, 2.6, 300)
x0, h = 1.15, 0.55
pts = np.array([x0 - h, x0, x0 + h]); fp = f(pts)
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 4.0), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.1})
for ax in (a1, a2):
    ax.plot(xs, f(xs), color=GRAY, lw=2.2, alpha=0.8)
    ax.plot(pts, fp, "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=9, zorder=5)
    ax.set_xticks(pts); ax.set_xticklabels([r"$x_{j-1}$", r"$x_j$", r"$x_{j+1}$"], fontsize=12.5)
    ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 2.6); ax.set_ylim(-0.62, 1.42)
t = np.array([x0 - 0.62, x0 + 0.62])
a1.plot(t, fp[1] + df(x0) * (t - x0), color="k", lw=1.6, ls="--", label=r"tangent at $x_j$: slope $\psi'(x_j)$")
sl = (fp[2] - fp[0]) / (2 * h)
a1.plot(t, fp[1] + sl * (t - x0), color=PURPLE, lw=2.4, label=r"slope of the chord: $(\psi_{j+1} - \psi_{j-1})/2h$")
a1.plot([pts[0], pts[2]], [fp[0], fp[2]], color=PURPLE, lw=1.4, ls=":")
a1.legend(loc="lower center", frameon=False, fontsize=11.5)
a1.set_title("first derivative: the slope of the chord", loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
a2.plot(pts[:2], fp[:2], color=ORANGE, lw=2.6, label=r"$s_- = (\psi_j - \psi_{j-1})/h$")
a2.plot(pts[1:], fp[1:], color=TEAL, lw=2.6, label=r"$s_+ = (\psi_{j+1} - \psi_j)/h$")
a2.legend(loc="lower left", frameon=False, fontsize=11.5, bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.13))
a2.text(0.01, 0.02, r"$\psi''(x_j) \approx \dfrac{s_+ - s_-}{h} = \dfrac{\psi_{j+1} - 2\psi_j + \psi_{j-1}}{h^2}$",
        transform=a2.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=12.5)
a2.set_title("second derivative: how much the slope changes", loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.91, bottom=0.09)
plt.show()

ddx  ⟶  D1=12h(0100−10100−10100−10),d2dx2  ⟶  D2=1h2(−21001−21001−21001−2)\frac{d}{dx} \;\longrightarrow\; D_1 = \frac{1}{2h}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \frac{d^2}{dx^2} \;\longrightarrow\; D_2 = \frac{1}{h^2}\begin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}dxd​⟶D1​=2h1​⎝⎛​0−100​10−10​010−1​0010​⎠⎞​,dx2d2​⟶D2​=h21​⎝⎛​−2100​1−210​01−21​001−2​⎠⎞​

  • Momentum is p^=−iℏ D1\hat{p} = -i\hbar\,D_1p^​=−iℏD1​: entries −iℏ/2h-i\hbar/2h−iℏ/2h above the diagonal and +iℏ/2h+i\hbar/2h+iℏ/2h below.

Example: the grid derivative of a plane wave

Apply the centered difference to the samples of a plane wave, ψj=eikxj\psi_j = e^{ikx_j}ψj​=eikxj​:

ψj+1−ψj−12h=eik(xj+h)−eik(xj−h)2h=eikh−e−ikh2h eikxj=isin⁡khh ψj\frac{\psi_{j+1} - \psi_{j-1}}{2h} = \frac{e^{ik(x_j + h)} - e^{ik(x_j - h)}}{2h} = \frac{e^{ikh} - e^{-ikh}}{2h}\,e^{ikx_j} = \frac{i\sin kh}{h}\,\psi_j2hψj+1​−ψj−1​​=2heik(xj​+h)−eik(xj​−h)​=2heikh−e−ikh​eikxj​=hisinkh​ψj​
(13)

The sampled plane wave is an eigenvector of the derivative matrix, just as eikxe^{ikx}eikx is an eigenfunction of d/dxd/dxd/dx (away from the ends of the grid). The eigenvalue isin⁡(kh)/hi\sin(kh)/hisin(kh)/h approaches the exact ikikik when the grid is fine, kh≪1kh \ll 1kh≪1. Multiplied by −iℏ-i\hbar−iℏ, the momentum matrix returns ℏsin⁡(kh)/h≈ℏk\hbar\sin(kh)/h \approx \hbar kℏsin(kh)/h≈ℏk, the de Broglie momentum. The grid works when it has many points per wavelength.

Step 4: the Hamiltonian is a matrix¶

  • Put the pieces together: H^=−ℏ22md2dx2+V(x)\hat{H} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + V(x)H^=−2mℏ2​dx2d2​+V(x) becomes H=−ℏ22mD2+VH = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}D_2 + VH=−2mℏ2​D2​+V. The constants in front of D2D_2D2​ collect into one symbol, ε=ℏ2/2mh2\varepsilon = \hbar^2/2mh^2ε=ℏ2/2mh2, which is only a unit of energy:

H=(2ε+V1−ε00−ε2ε+V2−ε00−ε2ε+V3−ε00−ε2ε+V4),ε=ℏ22mh2H = \begin{pmatrix} 2\varepsilon + V_1 & -\varepsilon & 0 & 0 \\ -\varepsilon & 2\varepsilon + V_2 & -\varepsilon & 0 \\ 0 & -\varepsilon & 2\varepsilon + V_3 & -\varepsilon \\ 0 & 0 & -\varepsilon & 2\varepsilon + V_4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{\hbar^2}{2mh^2}H=⎝⎛​2ε+V1​−ε00​−ε2ε+V2​−ε0​0−ε2ε+V3​−ε​00−ε2ε+V4​​⎠⎞​,ε=2mh2ℏ2​
(14)

  • Read it as a picture: the potential energy sits on the diagonal, one value per point, and the kinetic energy couples each point to its neighbors through −ε-\varepsilon−ε. This is the same structure as the Hückel matrix that chemists use for π\piπ electrons hopping between carbon atoms (Problem 6).

The Schrödinger equation on a grid
H^ψ=E ψ⟶Hv=E v\hat{H}\psi = E\,\psi \quad\longrightarrow\quad H\mathbf{v} = E\,\mathbf{v}H^ψ=Eψ⟶Hv=Ev
(15)

The allowed energies are the eigenvalues of the matrix HHH, and the stationary states are its eigenvectors: the wavefunctions sampled on the grid.

Example: a particle in a box with three grid points

Divide a box of length LLL into four intervals, h=L/4h = L/4h=L/4. The wavefunction vanishes at the two walls, which leaves three interior points, x=L/4x = L/4x=L/4, L/2L/2L/2 and 3L/43L/43L/4. With V=0V = 0V=0 inside,

H=ε(2−10−12−10−12),ε=ℏ22mh2=8ℏ2mL2H = \varepsilon\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{\hbar^2}{2mh^2} = \frac{8\hbar^2}{mL^2}H=ε⎝⎛​2−10​−12−1​0−12​⎠⎞​,ε=2mh2ℏ2​=mL28ℏ2​
(16)

Write E=λεE = \lambda\varepsilonE=λε and solve det⁡(H/ε−λI)=0\det(H/\varepsilon - \lambda I) = 0det(H/ε−λI)=0. Go along the first row: each entry times the 2×22\times 22×2 determinant that is left when its row and column are crossed out, with the signs + − ++\,-\,++−+:

(2−λ)[(2−λ)2−1]⏟row 1, column 1 crossed out−(−1)[−(2−λ)]⏟row 1, column 2 crossed out+0=(2−λ)[(2−λ)2−2]=0(2-\lambda)\underbrace{\big[(2-\lambda)^2 - 1\big]}_{\text{row 1, column 1 crossed out}} - (-1)\underbrace{\big[-(2-\lambda)\big]}_{\text{row 1, column 2 crossed out}} + 0 = (2-\lambda)\big[(2-\lambda)^2 - 2\big] = 0(2−λ)row 1, column 1 crossed out[(2−λ)2−1]​​−(−1)row 1, column 2 crossed out[−(2−λ)]​​+0=(2−λ)[(2−λ)2−2]=0
(17)

The product vanishes when λ=2\lambda = 2λ=2 or (2−λ)2=2(2 - \lambda)^2 = 2(2−λ)2=2, so λ=2−2, 2, 2+2\lambda = 2 - \sqrt{2},\ 2,\ 2 + \sqrt{2}λ=2−2​, 2, 2+2​. They add up to the trace, 6, and multiply to the determinant, 4. The lowest level is E1=(2−2) ε=4.69 ℏ2/mL2E_1 = (2 - \sqrt{2})\,\varepsilon = 4.69\,\hbar^2/mL^2E1​=(2−2​)ε=4.69ℏ2/mL2, within 5 percent of the exact π2ℏ2/2mL2=4.93 ℏ2/mL2\pi^2\hbar^2/2mL^2 = 4.93\,\hbar^2/mL^2π2ℏ2/2mL2=4.93ℏ2/mL2.

A row-times-column check confirms the ground state. Sample the exact ground state sin⁡(πx/L)\sin(\pi x/L)sin(πx/L) at the three points, (sin⁡π4,sin⁡π2,sin⁡3π4)∝(1,2,1)\big(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\big) \propto (1, \sqrt{2}, 1)(sin4π​,sin2π​,sin43π​)∝(1,2​,1):

(2−10−12−10−12)(121)=(2−222−22−2)=(2−2)(121)\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - \sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{2} - 2 \\ 2 - \sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} = (2 - \sqrt{2})\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}⎝⎛​2−10​−12−1​0−12​⎠⎞​⎝⎛​12​1​⎠⎞​=⎝⎛​2−2​22​−22−2​​⎠⎞​=(2−2​)⎝⎛​12​1​⎠⎞​
(18)

The middle entry works because 22−2=(2−2)22\sqrt{2} - 2 = (2 - \sqrt{2})\sqrt{2}22​−2=(2−2​)2​. The grid’s ground state is the exact sine, sampled at the grid points.

Fig. Left: the three eigenvectors of the three-point box (dots, joined by straight lines) on top of the exact box states (gray). Each is the exact sine sampled at the grid points. Right: the levels of grids with 3, 10 and 30 points against the exact ones, in units of ℏ2/mL2\hbar^2/mL^2ℏ2/mL2. More points give more levels, and each converges to the exact value from below. The top levels of a coarse grid are the least accurate, because their short wavelengths have few points per wavelength.

Example: five lines of numpy to solve the 1D Schrödinger equation

With 400 points instead of 3, the eigenvalue problem is too big for a determinant by hand, and numpy solves it in one call. Here is the particle on a spring whose levels you hunted with the trial-energy slider in The Schrödinger Equation, in units with ℏ=m=ω=1\hbar = m = \omega = 1ℏ=m=ω=1:

import numpy as np

N = 400                                       # grid points
x = np.linspace(-8, 8, N); h = x[1] - x[0]
D2 = (np.eye(N, k=1) - 2 * np.eye(N) + np.eye(N, k=-1)) / h**2    # second derivative
H = -0.5 * D2 + np.diag(0.5 * x**2)           # kinetic + potential energy

E, psi = np.linalg.eigh(H)                    # eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Hermitian matrix
print(np.round(E[:5], 4))                     # exact: 0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5 4.5
[0.4999 1.4997 2.4993 3.4987 4.4979]

  • The levels come out 0.5,1.5,2.5,…0.5, 1.5, 2.5, \dots0.5,1.5,2.5,… in units of ℏω\hbar\omegaℏω, to three or four digits. This evenly spaced ladder is the vibrating bond of Chapter 4. The columns of psi are the wavefunctions.

  • eigh is numpy’s eigensolver for Hermitian matrices. Why the physics hands us only Hermitian matrices is the subject of Operators 2.

Dirac notation¶

Integrals and matrices are two ways of writing the same objects. Dirac’s notation writes them once.

Kets and bras¶

  • A state is a ket ∣ψ⟩\lvert\psi\rangle∣ψ⟩: on the grid, the column of samples (ψ1,ψ2,… )(\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots)(ψ1​,ψ2​,…). Its partner, the bra ⟨ψ∣\langle\psi\rvert⟨ψ∣, is the same numbers written as a row, each one conjugated.

  • A bra next to a ket is an inner product, a single number:

⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩=∑jϕj∗ ψj h  ⟶  ∫ϕ∗ ψ dx\langle \phi \vert \psi \rangle = \sum_j \phi_j^*\,\psi_j\,h \;\longrightarrow\; \int \phi^*\,\psi\,dx⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩=j∑​ϕj∗​ψj​h⟶∫ϕ∗ψdx
(19)
Example: why the bra is conjugated

Take the two-component ket ∣ψ⟩=(1i)\lvert\psi\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{pmatrix}∣ψ⟩=(1i​). Its bra is ⟨ψ∣=(1, −i)\langle\psi\rvert = (1,\ -i)⟨ψ∣=(1, −i), so

⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=1⋅1+(−i)(i)=1+1=2\langle \psi \vert \psi \rangle = 1\cdot 1 + (-i)(i) = 1 + 1 = 2⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=1⋅1+(−i)(i)=1+1=2
(20)

a real, positive length squared. Without the conjugate the same product would be 1⋅1+i⋅i=01\cdot 1 + i\cdot i = 01⋅1+i⋅i=0: a nonzero vector of zero length. Conjugating the bra makes every ⟨ψ∣ψ⟩\langle \psi \vert \psi \rangle⟨ψ∣ψ⟩ real and positive, which is what allows ∣ψ∣2\lvert\psi\rvert^2∣ψ∣2 to be a probability density.

  • One consequence is used all the time: a number comes out of a ket unchanged but out of a bra conjugated, ⟨ϕ∣c ψ⟩=c ⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩\langle \phi \vert c\,\psi \rangle = c\,\langle \phi \vert \psi \rangle⟨ϕ∣cψ⟩=c⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩ but ⟨c ϕ∣ψ⟩=c∗⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩\langle c\,\phi \vert \psi \rangle = c^*\langle \phi \vert \psi \rangle⟨cϕ∣ψ⟩=c∗⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩, because ∫(c ϕ)∗ψ dx=c∗ ⁣∫ϕ∗ψ dx\int (c\,\phi)^*\psi\,dx = c^*\!\int \phi^*\psi\,dx∫(cϕ)∗ψdx=c∗∫ϕ∗ψdx.

Sandwiches: matrix elements¶

  • An operator acts on a ket, A^∣ψ⟩\hat{A}\lvert\psi\rangleA^∣ψ⟩: on the grid, the matrix times the column. Put a bra in front and the result is a number, the matrix element ⟨ϕ∣A^∣ψ⟩=∫ϕ∗ A^ψ dx\langle\phi\vert\hat{A}\vert\psi\rangle = \int\phi^*\,\hat{A}\psi\,dx⟨ϕ∣A^∣ψ⟩=∫ϕ∗A^ψdx: row times matrix times column.

  • The name is literal. Sandwiching a matrix between unit vectors picks out one entry. For A=(2112)A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​), e1=(1,0)\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)e1​=(1,0) and e2=(0,1)\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1)e2​=(0,1): Ae2=(1,2)A\mathbf{e}_2 = (1, 2)Ae2​=(1,2) and e1⋅(1,2)=1=A12\mathbf{e}_1\cdot(1, 2) = 1 = A_{12}e1​⋅(1,2)=1=A12​. In general Ajk=⟨ej∣A∣ek⟩A_{jk} = \langle \mathbf{e}_j \vert A \vert \mathbf{e}_k \rangleAjk​=⟨ej​∣A∣ek​⟩.

  • In a basis of functions instead of grid points, the same sandwich builds the matrices that quantum chemistry programs diagonalize: Hmn=⟨ϕm∣H^∣ϕn⟩H_{mn} = \langle \phi_m \vert \hat{H} \vert \phi_n \rangleHmn​=⟨ϕm​∣H^∣ϕn​⟩ for a set of orbitals ϕn\phi_nϕn​ (Hückel Theory).

Diagonalizing a Hamiltonian¶

  • The entries of a matrix depend on the axes you write it in; the operator does not. Turn the axes to perpendicular unit vectors u1,u2,…\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \dotsu1​,u2​,… and each entry becomes a sandwich, Amn′=⟨um∣A∣un⟩A'_{mn} = \langle \mathbf{u}_m \vert A \vert \mathbf{u}_n \rangleAmn′​=⟨um​∣A∣un​⟩. A Matrix in New Axes in Appendix A lets you turn the axes yourself and watch the entries change.

A matrix is diagonal in the axes of its eigenvectors
⟨um∣A∣un⟩=λn δmn\langle \mathbf{u}_m \vert A \vert \mathbf{u}_n \rangle = \lambda_n\,\delta_{mn}⟨um​∣A∣un​⟩=λn​δmn​
(21)

when the un\mathbf{u}_nun​ are perpendicular unit eigenvectors, Aun=λnunA\mathbf{u}_n = \lambda_n\mathbf{u}_nAun​=λn​un​. The symbol δmn\delta_{mn}δmn​ is 1 for m=nm = nm=n and 0 otherwise, so the eigenvalues sit on the diagonal and everything else is zero.

  • This is what diagonalizing a Hamiltonian means: finding the axes, its eigenvectors, in which HHH is diagonal. The diagonal then lists the energies. For the three-point box it holds 2−22 - \sqrt{2}2−2​, 2 and 2+22 + \sqrt{2}2+2​ in units of ε\varepsilonε, the energies found by hand above.

  • numpy finds the axes in one call. E, U = np.linalg.eigh(H) returns the eigenvectors as the columns of U, and U.T @ H @ U is HHH in those axes: diagonal, with E on the diagonal. A complex matrix needs the conjugate in the bra, U.conj().T @ H @ U. Measurement uses the same idea to expand a wavefunction along the eigenfunctions of an operator.

One language, three dialects¶

integralDiracnumpy on a grid
inner product∫ϕ∗ψ dx\int \phi^*\psi\,dx∫ϕ∗ψdx⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩\langle \phi \vert \psi \rangle⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩np.vdot(phi, psi) * h
normalization∫∣ψ∣2dx=1\int \lvert\psi\rvert^2 dx = 1∫∣ψ∣2dx=1⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=1\langle \psi \vert \psi \rangle = 1⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=1np.vdot(psi, psi) * h
operator actsA^ψ(x)\hat{A}\psi(x)A^ψ(x)A^∣ψ⟩\hat{A}\lvert\psi\rangleA^∣ψ⟩A @ psi
matrix element∫ϕ∗A^ψ dx\int \phi^*\hat{A}\psi\,dx∫ϕ∗A^ψdx⟨ϕ∣A^∣ψ⟩\langle \phi \vert \hat{A} \vert \psi \rangle⟨ϕ∣A^∣ψ⟩np.vdot(phi, A @ psi) * h
eigenvalue problemA^ϕn=anϕn\hat{A}\phi_n = a_n\phi_nA^ϕn​=an​ϕn​A^∣n⟩=an∣n⟩\hat{A}\lvert n\rangle = a_n\lvert n\rangleA^∣n⟩=an​∣n⟩a, phi = np.linalg.eigh(A)
matrix in new axesAmn′=∫ϕm∗A^ϕn dxA'_{mn} = \int \phi_m^*\hat{A}\phi_n\,dxAmn′​=∫ϕm∗​A^ϕn​dxAmn′=⟨ϕm∣A^∣ϕn⟩A'_{mn} = \langle \phi_m \vert \hat{A} \vert \phi_n \rangleAmn′​=⟨ϕm​∣A^∣ϕn​⟩U.conj().T @ A @ U * h (columns of U: the ϕn\phi_nϕn​)

  • np.vdot conjugates its first argument, which is exactly what the bra does. The factor h turns the sum over grid points into the integral.

  • The table grows in the next three lectures: adjoints and commutators in Operators 2, expansion coefficients in Measurement, time evolution in Time Dependence.

Two matrix properties to watch¶

Here are x^\hat{x}x^, p^\hat{p}p^​ and H^\hat{H}H^ for a particle on a spring on an 8-point grid, as color maps. At any size they keep the same pattern:

Source
# synced: grid_operators
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
div = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", [TEAL, "white", CARDINAL])
N = 8                                                       # hbar = m = 1, V = x^2/2 on 8 points
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, N); h = x[1] - x[0]
up, dn = np.eye(N, k=1), np.eye(N, k=-1)
X = np.diag(x)
P = -1j * (up - dn) / (2 * h)                               # p = -i d/dx as a centered difference
H = -0.5 * (up - 2 * np.eye(N) + dn) / h**2 + np.diag(0.5 * x**2)
panels = [(X, r"$\hat{x}$", "grid positions on the diagonal\nreal, symmetric"),
          (P.imag, r"$\hat{p}$  (imaginary part)", r"$\mp i\hbar/2h$ next to the diagonal" + "\nimaginary, antisymmetric"),
          (H, r"$\hat{H}$", "$V$ on the diagonal, neighbors linked\nreal, symmetric")]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.6, 3.8))
for ax, (M, title, note) in zip(axs, panels):
    m = np.abs(M).max()
    ax.imshow(M, cmap=div, vmin=-m, vmax=m)
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, N, 1), minor=True); ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, N, 1), minor=True)
    ax.grid(which="minor", color="white", lw=1.5)
    ax.tick_params(which="both", length=0, labelbottom=False, labelleft=False)
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_visible(False)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=14)
    ax.set_xlabel(note, fontsize=11.5, linespacing=1.4)
fig.suptitle(r"each matrix equals its conjugate transpose: $A^\dagger = A$", fontsize=13, y=0.98)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.98, top=0.83, bottom=0.17, wspace=0.18)
plt.show()

Fig. Position, momentum and energy of a particle on a spring, on a grid of 8 points. Color shows the sign and size of each entry (teal negative, red positive, white zero). Each matrix equals its own conjugate transpose, the defining property of a Hermitian matrix (Operators 2); momentum manages it with an imaginary, antisymmetric pattern.

  • Mirror symmetry. Each of these matrices equals its own mirror image across the diagonal, after conjugating the entries. Matrices like this are called Hermitian, and Operators 2 shows why every observable must be one: it guarantees real eigenvalues.

  • Order. Matrix products depend on the order, AB≠BAAB \neq BAAB=BA in general, and on the grid XP≠PXXP \neq PXXP=PX. The difference, the commutator, decides which observables can be sharp at the same time (Operators 2).

Problems¶

Problem 1: Linear or not?¶

Decide which of these operators are linear: (a) A^f=f+x\hat{A}f = f + xA^f=f+x, (b) B^f=x2 d2fdx2\hat{B}f = x^2\,\dfrac{d^2f}{dx^2}B^f=x2dx2d2f​, (c) C^f=∫0xf(y) dy\hat{C}f = \displaystyle\int_0^x f(y)\,dyC^f=∫0x​f(y)dy, (d) D^f=ef\hat{D}f = e^{f}D^f=ef.

Solution

  • (a) Not linear. A^(2f)=2f+x\hat{A}(2f) = 2f + xA^(2f)=2f+x, but 2A^f=2f+2x2\hat{A}f = 2f + 2x2A^f=2f+2x. Adding something that does not depend on fff always breaks linearity.

  • (b) Linear. The second derivative of a sum is the sum of the second derivatives, and multiplying by x2x^2x2 keeps constants and sums intact.

  • (c) Linear. The integral of c1f1+c2f2c_1f_1 + c_2f_2c1​f1​+c2​f2​ is c1∫f1+c2∫f2c_1\int f_1 + c_2\int f_2c1​∫f1​+c2​∫f2​.

  • (d) Not linear. ef1+f2=ef1ef2e^{f_1 + f_2} = e^{f_1}e^{f_2}ef1​+f2​=ef1​ef2​, a product rather than a sum.

Problem 2: Eigenvectors by hand¶

Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of B=(222−1)B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}B=(22​2−1​). Check them against the trace and the determinant, and check that the two eigenvectors are perpendicular.

Solution
det⁡(B−λI)=(2−λ)(−1−λ)−4=λ2−λ−6=(λ−3)(λ+2)=0⟹λ=3, −2\det(B - \lambda I) = (2 - \lambda)(-1 - \lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 - \lambda - 6 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 2) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = 3,\ -2det(B−λI)=(2−λ)(−1−λ)−4=λ2−λ−6=(λ−3)(λ+2)=0⟹λ=3, −2
(22)

For λ=3\lambda = 3λ=3 the first row of (B−3I)v=0(B - 3I)\mathbf{v} = 0(B−3I)v=0 reads −v1+2v2=0-v_1 + 2v_2 = 0−v1​+2v2​=0, so v∝(2,1)\mathbf{v} \propto (2, 1)v∝(2,1). For λ=−2\lambda = -2λ=−2 it reads 4v1+2v2=04v_1 + 2v_2 = 04v1​+2v2​=0, so v∝(1,−2)\mathbf{v} \propto (1, -2)v∝(1,−2). Checks: 3+(−2)=13 + (-2) = 13+(−2)=1 is the trace 2+(−1)2 + (-1)2+(−1), and 3×(−2)=−63 \times (-2) = -63×(−2)=−6 is the determinant 2⋅(−1)−2⋅22\cdot(-1) - 2\cdot 22⋅(−1)−2⋅2. The dot product (2,1)⋅(1,−2)=0(2, 1)\cdot(1, -2) = 0(2,1)⋅(1,−2)=0, so the eigenvectors are perpendicular, a property of every symmetric matrix that Operators 2 explains.

Problem 3: Two orbitals, one matrix¶

In Hückel theory the two ppp orbitals of ethylene are described by H=(αββα)H = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \beta \\ \beta & \alpha \end{pmatrix}H=(αβ​βα​), where α\alphaα is the energy of an electron on one carbon and β<0\beta < 0β<0 couples the two. Find the energies and the normalized eigenvectors. Which combination is lower in energy?

Solution

det⁡(H−EI)=(α−E)2−β2=0\det(H - EI) = (\alpha - E)^2 - \beta^2 = 0det(H−EI)=(α−E)2−β2=0, so α−E=±β\alpha - E = \pm\betaα−E=±β and E=α+βE = \alpha + \betaE=α+β or E=α−βE = \alpha - \betaE=α−β. For E=α+βE = \alpha + \betaE=α+β the first row of (H−EI)v=0(H - EI)\mathbf{v} = 0(H−EI)v=0 reads −βv1+βv2=0-\beta v_1 + \beta v_2 = 0−βv1​+βv2​=0, so v=(1,1)/2\mathbf{v} = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}v=(1,1)/2​; for E=α−βE = \alpha - \betaE=α−β, v=(1,−1)/2\mathbf{v} = (1, -1)/\sqrt{2}v=(1,−1)/2​. Since β<0\beta < 0β<0, α+β\alpha + \betaα+β is the lower energy: the in-phase combination (1,1)/2(1, 1)/\sqrt{2}(1,1)/2​ is the bonding orbital, and the out-of-phase (1,−1)/2(1, -1)/\sqrt{2}(1,−1)/2​, with a node between the carbons, is antibonding. The eigenvectors do not depend on α\alphaα or β\betaβ at all; the symmetry of the molecule fixes them.

Problem 4: Position as a matrix in the box basis¶

Use the box states ψn=2/L sin⁡(nπx/L)\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(n\pi x/L)ψn​=2/L​sin(nπx/L) as a basis and build the 3×33\times 33×3 matrix xmn=⟨ψm∣x^∣ψn⟩x_{mn} = \langle \psi_m \vert \hat{x} \vert \psi_n \ranglexmn​=⟨ψm​∣x^∣ψn​⟩, m,n=1,2,3m, n = 1, 2, 3m,n=1,2,3, with numpy on a grid. Is the matrix symmetric? Which entries vanish?

Solution
import numpy as np
L = 1.0
x = np.linspace(0, L, 2001); h = x[1] - x[0]
psi = np.array([np.sqrt(2 / L) * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L) for n in (1, 2, 3)])
X = np.array([[np.sum(psi[m] * x * psi[n]) * h for n in range(3)] for m in range(3)])
print(np.round(X, 4))   # [[ 0.5 -0.1801 0. ] [-0.1801 0.5 -0.1945] [ 0. -0.1945 0.5]]

Each diagonal entry is ⟨x⟩=L/2\langle x \rangle = L/2⟨x⟩=L/2, because every box state is symmetric about the middle of the box. The matrix is symmetric, xmn=xnmx_{mn} = x_{nm}xmn​=xnm​, as a real operator in a real basis must be. The entries x13=x31x_{13} = x_{31}x13​=x31​ vanish: write x=(x−L/2)+L/2x = (x - L/2) + L/2x=(x−L/2)+L/2; the L/2L/2L/2 part gives L2⟨ψ1∣ψ3⟩=0\tfrac{L}{2}\langle \psi_1 \vert \psi_3 \rangle = 02L​⟨ψ1​∣ψ3​⟩=0, and in the other part ψ1ψ3\psi_1\psi_3ψ1​ψ3​ is symmetric about L/2L/2L/2 while x−L/2x - L/2x−L/2 is antisymmetric, so the two halves of the integral cancel.

Then show that its eigenvalues are λ=cos⁡θ±isin⁡θ=e±iθ\lambda = \cos\theta \pm i\sin\theta = e^{\pm i\theta}λ=cosθ±isinθ=e±iθ, find the eigenvectors, and say for which angles the eigenvalues are real.
